definition: Emergency roof repair stabilizes a sudden roof failure — an active leak, storm-stripped shingles, a fallen-tree puncture, or ice-dam backup — to stop water entry before the loss compounds. It tarps or patches the breach first, then schedules the permanent repair.

signs: Water entering through a ceiling, wall, or light fixture during or after rainfall indicates an active roof breach and ranks as an immediate stabilization priority, because wet materials dried within 24–48 hours of a leak in most cases grow no mold — per the EPA.

Shingles or membrane stripped from a roof section after high wind exposes the underlayment and roof deck to the next rainfall; a thunderstorm is classed as severe at wind gusts of 58 mph or higher — per NOAA. (3-tab shingles carry roughly a 60 mph rating and architectural shingles rate up to 130 mph — per ARMA and manufacturer guidance.)

A fallen tree, large branch, or wind-driven debris penetrating the roof covering opens the structure to water and falls in the largest homeowners-insurance claim type, wind and hail, at 1 in 36 insured homes per year — per the Insurance Information Institute (Triple-I).

Daylight or a sagging roofline visible from inside the attic indicates deck or framing compromise, a structural priority that points toward replacement rather than a patch — per GAF inspection guidance.

Icicles and thick ice ridges at the eaves with interior stains near the top-floor exterior walls indicate an ice dam backing meltwater under the shingles, a winter pattern driven by attic heat escape — per University of Minnesota Extension.

Ponding water held on a low-slope roof for more than 48 hours after rain counts as a defect that breaks down membrane seams; a flat roof needs at least 1/4 inch per foot of slope to drain — per NRCA and ARMA.
selectionCriteria: Active New Jersey Home Improvement Contractor registration (N.J.S.A. 56:8-136) — this is a REGISTRATION, not a license; New Jersey issues no roofing license. Verify the 13VH registration number, which must appear on the contract and in advertising per N.J.S.A. 56:8-144.
Commercial general liability insurance of at least $500,000 per occurrence (N.J.S.A. 56:8-142), verified by requesting a Certificate of Insurance directly from the carrier.
A written contract for any work over $500, signed by both parties, with the start/completion dates and total price (N.J.A.C. 13:45A-16.2).
A detailed, itemized WRITTEN estimate that separates the emergency stabilization (tarp/patch) scope from the permanent repair scope, rather than a single verbal number under pressure.
A verifiable local physical address and established Essex County presence with checkable local references — not a door-to-door, post-storm, out-of-state-plate operator.

A thorough, documented assessment: an inspection of the roof and attic that identifies the active entry point and confirms whether the framing carries the covering, with timestamped photographs recorded for the insurance adjuster.
Manufacturer-approved bonding on membrane and component repairs so an existing system warranty stays intact (a contractor practice, NOT a manufacturer-certification self-claim by NQR).

technicalFacts.fact: Wet materials dried within 24–48 hours of a leak in most cases grow no mold, so every hour of water exposure raises the secondary-damage cost — which is why stabilization (tarp/patch) is sequenced ahead of the permanent repair.
A thunderstorm is classified as severe at wind gusts of 58 mph or higher — the threshold that strips shingles and tears membrane seams.
3-tab shingles carry roughly a 60 mph wind rating while architectural shingles rate up to 130 mph.

Wind and hail is the largest homeowners-insurance claim type at 2.8% of insured homes per year (1 in 36), with an average claim of $14,747; water damage and freezing follow at 1 in 67 with an average claim of $15,400.
An emergency roof tarp protects a building for roughly 30 days — the design span fiber-reinforced emergency sheeting is rated for — bridging until the permanent repair.
technicalFacts.source: FEMA and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Operation Blue Roof program

technicalFacts.fact: Temporary emergency protection covers a roof with no more than 50% of the framing damaged; above that threshold a roof needs a structural rebuild rather than a tarp-and-repair scope.
technicalFacts.source: FEMA and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Operation Blue Roof program

technicalFacts.fact: Repair or replacement of the roof covering on a detached one- and two-family dwelling counts as ordinary maintenance — no construction permit, inspection, or notice to the construction official required.

On a commercial building, repairing more than 25% of the total roof area in a 12-month period requires a permit; an emergency scope therefore separates the stabilization patch from the permitted permanent repair.
Ponding water held on a low-slope roof more than 48 hours after rain counts as a defect; a flat roof needs at least 1/4 inch per foot of slope to drain.

Membrane life expectancy on commercial low-slope roofs: EPDM 15–25 years, TPO 7–20 years, modified bitumen 20 years — an emergency membrane patch reseals the storm-opened seam where these systems fail.
Nor'easters bring sustained winds up to 60 mph; New Jersey averages at least one coastal storm per year (some years 5–10), most common October through April.
technicalFacts.source: NJ Office of the Governor; NOAA New Jersey State Climate Summary

technicalFacts.fact: Ice-dam meltwater backup is a winter pattern driven by attic heat escape (not by gutters or ventilation as the root cause).

Do NOT reproduce manufacturer brand-system lines ('Firestone, Carlisle, Johns Manville membrane systems' or 'GAF, CertainTeed, Owens Corning shingle systems'). Membranes may be named generically (EPDM, TPO, modified bitumen) without asserting a brand partnership or installer certification.

24/7 VERIFICATION CONCLUSION (from the SERVICE NOTE): The gold does NOT support a 24/7 claim — its only stated hours are Mon–Fri 7:00 AM–6:00 PM and Sat 8:00 AM–2:00 PM (gold whyChooseUs 'Local Essex County Roofers'). AUTHOR INSTRUCTION: never write '24/7' or any around-the-clock staffing promise. Frame the value as rapid emergency response with stabilization-first (tarp/patch to stop water entry, then schedule the permanent repair), justified by the EPA 24–48-hour mold-dry-out window. The honest tarp-duration fact is ~30 days (FEMA/USACE Operation Blue Roof), and the structural cutoff for tarp-and-repair vs. rebuild is no more than 50% framing damage.

Cost: AUTHOR INSTRUCTION — there is NO whole-job emergency total in the gold; hasRealWholeProjectTotal is false. Price ONLY per-repair/per-component with named sources ($200–$1,000+ most repairs + 25–50% premium / $400–$1,000 standard leak / $200–$500 flashing reseal), then point to NQR's free written estimate. Do not invent a tarping price band, a tree-strike total, or a trip fee.
